title: Dance Like Nobodys Watching

jokes.text: Have you ever put out a cigar on Gilbert Gottfried's neck? Because I have, and his screams were the worst thing I'd ever heard. Until tonight.
jokes.setup: Jack appears to be complimenting a contestant, building in an increasingly over-the-top direction with the Gilbert Gottfried anecdote
jokes.punchline: 'Until tonight' — the digression about Gottfried's screams turns out to be a setup for the most brutal possible comparison, landing a devastating insult
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional Jack Donaghy character comedy — only he would escalate a reality-show critique by invoking a Gilbert Gottfried neck-cigar story. The misdirection is perfectly structured: we think it's a bizarre tangent, then 'Until tonight' snaps it into a brutal insult. Deeply character-specific, economical, dark, and original. Earns its 8+ because it uses Jack's sociopathic patrician cruelty at its sharpest.

jokes.text: Also, Jason, if you think you're passing for straight, you're embarrassing yourself.
jokes.setup: Jack has just rolled his ankle and is in mild physical distress
jokes.punchline: Mid-pain, he fires off a completely casual, unprompted aside to the contestant about his gayness, as if it's merely another critique to deliver
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in Jack's casual delivery — he's literally hopping on a rolled ankle and still finds time to dispense unsolicited blunt feedback. Pure character integration. The 'Also' is doing enormous work, making it feel like an afterthought on his to-do list.

jokes.text: Did you know that both her mothers are serial killers?
jokes.setup: The conversation is about why audiences love contestant Shayla's 'personal story'
jokes.punchline: The 'personal story' turns out to be that both of her mothers are serial killers — a completely absurdist escalation of reality TV sob-story tropes
jokes.explanation: A perfect 30 Rock joke — it satirizes reality TV's exploitation of contestants' hardships by taking it to an absurd extreme. 'Both her mothers' does double duty, acknowledging a same-sex couple and then immediately making them both serial killers. Punchy, original, economical.

jokes.text: That's America. [cut to new scene]
jokes.setup: Someone has just revealed that both of Shayla's mothers are serial killers, which apparently explains her popularity
jokes.punchline: 'That's America.' — delivered as a complete, satisfied explanation, followed by an immediate scene cut
jokes.explanation: Two words that land as a perfectly timed button. The scene cut immediately after maximizes the joke — there's no over-explanation. Scathing media satire compressed into five syllables. Perfect economy score.

jokes.text: Of course. A little less than my kidnapped wife, but I did get a nice Christmas card from Avery and Kim Jong-Un.
jokes.setup: Liz asks if Jack missed her over the break, expecting a normal answer
jokes.punchline: Jack quantifies his feelings precisely ('a little less than my kidnapped wife'), then reveals he got a Christmas card from his hostage wife and Kim Jong-Un — treating a geopolitical abduction as a mild holiday inconvenience
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a high-water mark for 30 Rock's layered absurdism. It does three things at once: (1) precisely quantifies Jack's emotional affect in a hilariously clinical way, (2) casually reintroduces the Avery/Kim Jong-Un plotline as if it were a minor scheduling conflict, and (3) the 'nice Christmas card' from a dictator holding his wife hostage is a perfectly calibrated dark absurdist image. Only Jack Donaghy can deliver this. Earns its 8+ comfortably.

jokes.text: She's like a little human tumbler of scotch.
jokes.setup: Jack is expressing affection for his infant daughter Liddy
jokes.punchline: The warmest compliment he can conceive of is comparing her to a small portion of his preferred alcoholic beverage
jokes.explanation: This joke could only be said by Jack Donaghy. It's simultaneously a tender declaration of fatherly love AND a perfect encapsulation of his character in one image. The specificity ('tumbler' rather than just 'glass') shows craft. Highly quotable and earns its 8+ through character integration and originality.

jokes.text: You turning soft on me, Donaghy? If you want, I can recommend a good gynecologist. You know, 'cause I really like my guy. He's sort of a doogie howser type. But younger.
jokes.setup: Liz mocks Jack for going soft, offers a gynecologist recommendation as a joke, then undermines her own insult by genuinely praising hers
jokes.punchline: 'He's sort of a doogie howser type. But younger.' — the insult completely collapses into Liz accidentally oversharing sincere medical opinions
jokes.explanation: Classic Liz Lemon joke structure: she starts with a sharp burn, then can't help herself from genuinely engaging with the tangent, making herself look more awkward than Jack. 'But younger' as a button is perfectly economical — it raises more questions than it answers and shows Liz cheerfully describing a disturbingly young doctor without registering why that's odd.

jokes.text: Jack predicts Liz's entire holiday in exact detail — eggnog alcohol mistake, shoving match with aunt over star, 'It was my year!', lupus/line-cutting, two bad sweaters, wrong War WWII book for Dad.
jokes.setup: Liz is about to tell Jack how her holidays were
jokes.punchline: Jack cuts her off and narrates her entire holiday with perfect precision, detail by depressing detail, each one landing as its own micro-joke
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in sustained character comedy. Each beat Jack adds is funnier and sadder than the last — the eggnog mistake shows Liz's naivety, the lupus line-cutter is delightfully specific, and the wrong WWII book is the perfect cap of mundane pathos. The joke works because it reveals both Jack's intimate knowledge of Liz AND how predictably miserable her life is. Earns 8+ through structure and character integration.

jokes.text: What, lupus lets you just cut the line?
jokes.setup: Jack narrates that Liz had a shoving match with her aunt about who puts the star on top of the tree
jokes.punchline: Liz's outburst of 'It was my year!' is followed by this — revealing she genuinely fought with a lupus patient over a Christmas decoration
jokes.explanation: One of the most quotable lines in the episode. It's a tiny joke doing enormous work: Liz frames lupus as an unfair competitive advantage in a Christmas ritual, which is both dark and completely true to her oblivious selfishness. Perfect economy. Highly quotable standalone line.

jokes.text: Take off that jacket. If you're not wearing one of those Christmas sweaters out of guilt, I'll give you $1,000.
jokes.setup: Liz insists Jack doesn't know everything about her
jokes.punchline: Jack is so certain about the guilt sweaters that he offers $1,000 on the spot
jokes.explanation: Solid setup for the punchline that follows. Jack's unshakeable confidence in predicting Liz is well-established and the $1,000 bet shows his contempt for the concept of being wrong. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Wrong, Jack. 'Cause they weren't sweaters. They were Dickies!
jokes.setup: Jack bets $1,000 she's wearing guilt Christmas sweaters under her jacket
jokes.punchline: She triumphantly reveals they're Dickies — a brand of workwear that is somehow even sadder and more Liz-coded than Christmas sweaters
jokes.explanation: The perfect payoff to the sweater setup. The joke works on two levels: Liz is genuinely pleased to have 'won' by revealing she's wearing Dickies (workwear) instead of Christmas sweaters, without realizing that Dickies are objectively worse and more pathetic. Her oblivious triumph IS the joke. 'Happy 2012!' as a button is a perfect non-sequitur mic drop. Earns 8+ through character integration and the beautiful irony of her victory.

jokes.text: I'm sorry you're going to hell. That's okay. How was your break?
jokes.setup: Kenneth approaches Mr. Rossitano in the hallway
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's 'I'm sorry you're going to hell' is delivered with the same casual warmth as 'I'm sorry for your loss,' and Rossitano's 'That's okay. How was your break?' treats damnation as a minor conversational speed bump
jokes.explanation: A beautifully compact exchange. Kenneth's religiosity has been established over seasons, and the joke works because his condolence about hell is genuinely sincere and warm. Rossitano's total non-reaction is the second punchline — he treats the damnation prediction the same way you'd respond to 'your fly's down.' Perfect economy.

jokes.text: The world is ending tomorrow! / And you're happy about that? / Oh, of course. I get to go to heaven and receive my reward! 72 virgin margaritas, hold the salt.
jokes.setup: Kenneth's preacher has calculated the end of the world is tomorrow; someone asks if he's happy about that
jokes.punchline: '72 virgin margaritas, hold the salt' — a riff on the Islamic 72 virgins belief, filtered through Kenneth's Southern Baptist sensibility into a teetotaling cocktail order
jokes.explanation: Exceptional joke. It conflates two religious traditions (Christian rapture + Islamic paradise) in a way that's absurd but internally logical for Kenneth — his heaven would naturally not involve actual virgins or actual alcohol. The 'hold the salt' detail is a perfect comic button. Highly quotable and original. Earns 8+ easily.

jokes.text: I'm sorry I won't be seeing you in heaven, Mr. Spurlock. But on the bright side, black hell does have a jukebox.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is saying farewell to colleagues he won't see in heaven
jokes.punchline: Kenneth casually reveals that hell is racially segregated, and he's thought through the amenities of 'black hell' (jukebox) as a consolation
jokes.explanation: A genuinely daring joke. It uses Kenneth's cheerful naivety to expose the casual racism embedded in certain strains of American Christianity, with the jukebox detail making it both more absurd and more pointed. The joke doesn't punch at Spurlock — it exposes Kenneth's worldview. Dark, original, and character-specific. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Is the sky blue? / Until tomorrow, when it will be on fire.
jokes.setup: Someone uses 'is the sky blue?' as a rhetorical affirmative
jokes.punchline: Kenneth literalizes it with a calm apocalyptic correction — yes, currently blue, tomorrow fire
jokes.explanation: A tight, elegant subversion of a cliché. The idiom 'is the sky blue?' exists as a rhetorical certainty, and Kenneth undermines it with cheerful specificity. The joke works on a comedy-writing level — taking a dead phrase and finding an unexpected new angle. Economical and well-structured.

jokes.text: I came across the following quote on the side of a tampon box this Christmas. 'Work like you don't need the money. Love like you've never been hurt. Dance like nobody's watching. Enjoy these satchel Paige brand tampons.'
jokes.setup: Liz is sharing an inspirational quote that moved her
jokes.punchline: The inspirational quote was on a tampon box — and the brand name ('Satchel Paige brand tampons') is absurdly specific and incongruous, suggesting a baseball legend's hygiene product line
jokes.explanation: Also the episode's title joke. A perfectly layered gag: the inspirational quote is undercut by its source (tampon box), but then the brand name 'Satchel Paige' adds a second layer of absurdity — a famous African-American baseball pitcher's name on tampons. The juxtaposition of genuinely moving words with product-placement cheerfulness is a 30 Rock signature move. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Also, maybe I'm in a good mood because I'm not being weighed down by redundant torso fabric. / What does that mean? / Wouldn't you like to know?
jokes.setup: Liz is explaining her good mood
jokes.punchline: 'Redundant torso fabric' is a bizarre euphemism that means nothing until we eventually understand she's dropped her bra for WNBA dancing freedom; her teasing non-answer 'Wouldn't you like to know?' adds to the mystery
jokes.explanation: A plant for a later payoff. 'Redundant torso fabric' is a genuinely funny phrase, and Liz's coy evasion is out of character enough to be funny. Gains rewatch value once the WNBA subplot is revealed. Scores modestly on first watch.

jokes.text: When you Google 'Jenna Maroney' now, I come up first. Not the Jenna Maroney who electrocuted all those horses.
jokes.setup: Jenna is celebrating her increased fame from the kids' singing show
jokes.punchline: Another Jenna Maroney exists who electrocuted horses — and Jenna's relief at outranking this person is more disturbing than the crime itself
jokes.explanation: An absolutely classic 30 Rock gag. The callback to Jenna being the horse-electrocutor ('Jenna, that was you') makes it even better. The joke has two punchlines: first the existence of a horse-electrocuting Jenna, then the revelation that it was our Jenna all along. Highly quotable and shows Jenna's obliviousness at its best.

jokes.text: Jenna, that was you.
jokes.setup: Jenna celebrates that she now outranks the Jenna Maroney who electrocuted horses on Google
jokes.punchline: Liz calmly informs her that she IS the horse-electrocuting Jenna
jokes.explanation: Four words. Perfect. Liz's flat delivery of 'Jenna, that was you' as Jenna completely fails to realize her own infamy is the second punchline of a two-stage joke and lands harder than the setup. Economy score is a 10 — you cannot do this in fewer words. One of the episode's sharpest moments.

jokes.text: Talent walking! / This has nothing to do with Jenna's success that I'm jealous of, but if that yellow-haired bag of teeth keeps me waiting for rehearsal, I will set my dressing room on fire.
jokes.setup: Tracy announces 'Talent walking!' to clear a path, then immediately undercuts himself
jokes.punchline: 'This has nothing to do with Jenna's success that I'm jealous of' — the denial is so transparently false it becomes the confession, followed by the absurd threat to burn his own dressing room
jokes.explanation: 'Yellow-haired bag of teeth' is a vivid, specific insult that elevates what could be a standard jealousy joke. Tracy's self-undermining denial is perfectly in character — he has no self-awareness filter.

jokes.text: But I'm acting out. / Right. And I know it'll all blow over eventually, and so I'm just going to skip the exhausting middle part.
jokes.setup: Tracy insists Liz needs to manage his acting out
jokes.punchline: Liz explicitly opts out of the show's standard Tracy-management formula, naming the 'exhausting middle part' as a process she's skipping
jokes.explanation: Smartly meta — Liz is essentially acknowledging the show's formula and refusing to participate. After six seasons, this lands for the audience who has watched the same dynamic play out dozens of times. Character-specific and economical.

jokes.text: You're a 42-year-old man. / No, I'm not. I took a real age test. It said I'm dead.
jokes.setup: Liz tries to invoke Tracy's adult responsibility
jokes.punchline: Tracy has taken a 'real age test' whose result was 'dead' — which he reports as a factual, slightly inconvenient finding
jokes.explanation: Tracy's logic is impeccable within his own reality — he took a legitimate test, the test had a result, he accepts it. The deadpan delivery of 'It said I'm dead' is what makes it work. Very Tracy-specific and highly quotable.

jokes.text: This week, America's kids sing really old songs that everyone knows and NBC doesn't have to pay for. / It's brilliant.
jokes.setup: Jack explains the concept of 'Public Domain Week'
jokes.punchline: The artistic conceit is entirely motivated by royalty avoidance — and Liz's 'It's brilliant' is completely sincere
jokes.explanation: Sharp corporate satire of reality TV economics dressed as innovation. Both characters are in on it in different ways — Jack proudly, Liz accidentally. Clean and economical.

jokes.text: Unlike cash cow, the failed NBC spin-off of cash cab.
jokes.setup: Jack calls the singing show 'a real cash cow'
jokes.punchline: Liz riffs on the phrase to reference a fake failed NBC show — 'Cash Cow,' a livestock version of the game show 'Cash Cab'
jokes.explanation: Wordplay-driven absurdism. The pun on 'cash cow' leads to a fake show that is both an obvious joke and somehow feels like NBC might actually have tried it. The meta-NBC mockery is a 30 Rock staple.

jokes.text: You try riding a cow through midtown Manhattan, Lemon. The animal will panic.
jokes.setup: Liz references the failed 'Cash Cow' spin-off
jokes.punchline: Jack responds as if the show's failure was a logistical cow-management problem he personally encountered — with the gravely serious observation that the animal panics in traffic
jokes.explanation: Jack commits completely to the bit, treating the logistics of riding a cow through midtown as a genuine operational failure he experienced firsthand. The specificity ('The animal will panic') is what makes it exceptional — it implies he tried it. This is 30 Rock absurdism at its finest. Only Jack Donaghy would have this specific problem. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: What if I told you your first match burned his groin off in an accident at his cake shop.
jokes.setup: Liz refuses to use the dating website Jack signed her up for
jokes.punchline: Jack dangles the irresistibly specific detail of a cake-shop groin accident as a selling point
jokes.explanation: The specificity ('cake shop' is funnier than 'bakery,' 'groin' is funnier than 'leg') does the heavy lifting. It also characterizes the dating site as truly desperate. Functional and punchy.

jokes.text: Die, you blonde bitch! / Thank you.
jokes.setup: Jenna walks through the studio toward the taping
jokes.punchline: An audience member screams 'Die, you blonde bitch!' and Jenna responds with a gracious 'Thank you,' treating hatred as applause
jokes.explanation: Two words ('Thank you') are the entire punchline, and they're perfect. Jenna accepts hatred as a form of celebrity acknowledgment. This is her character in miniature — so narcissistic that negative attention registers as positive. The economy here is near-perfect. Earns 8+ for structure and character integration.

jokes.text: Oh. Ha. That's odd, because my daughter's name... / I'm going to interrupt you right there.
jokes.setup: A stranger says their daughter is named Liddy; Jack begins to share that his daughter is also named Liddy
jokes.punchline: Jenna interrupts Jack mid-sentence to give a brutal critique of the child contestant — the cutoff is the joke, with Jenna treating a human moment as an obstacle to her feedback
jokes.explanation: Jenna's interruption of what would be a nice human moment is perfectly in character. The setup of the Liddy name coincidence is a red herring — we expect a warm connection, get brutality instead.

jokes.text: You're weird looking, Liddy. Even if you could sing, with that face it would be like eating a steak that just came out of a dumpster.
jokes.setup: Jenna is giving 'feedback' to a child contestant named Liddy
jokes.punchline: 'Like eating a steak that just came out of a dumpster' — a weirdly specific, almost philosophical metaphor for the experience of a talented but ugly person
jokes.explanation: The dumpster steak metaphor is unexpectedly specific and philosophical — it implies the steak IS good but the context ruins it. The reveal 'I've done that' from someone in the audience adds a bonus laugh.

jokes.text: I've done that. [referring to eating a dumpster steak]
jokes.setup: Jenna uses dumpster steak as a metaphor
jokes.punchline: An audience member confirms they have literally eaten a steak from a dumpster, treating the metaphor as a relatable experience
jokes.explanation: A quick secondary joke that lands as a bonus. Low character integration since it's an unnamed audience member, but the unexpected literalization of the metaphor is clean.

jokes.text: Take voice lessons. Then seal yourself in a barrel, and fall off of the waterfall.
jokes.setup: Jenna continues her 'advice' to the child Liddy
jokes.punchline: The advice escalates from normal ('take voice lessons') to 'seal yourself in a barrel and fall off a waterfall' — suggesting elaborate child murder as a career strategy
jokes.explanation: The escalation structure is key — it starts with legitimate advice and ends with a specific, elaborate suggestion for child death. The waterfall barrel detail is oddly specific in a way that implies historical knowledge of daredevil stunts, making it funnier. Dark and well-constructed.

jokes.text: Liddy, go jump back up your mother. / Go jump back up your mother, Liddy. / Yeah, I like the third one for me, and her crying on the second one.
jokes.setup: Jenna is recording a catchphrase to use on the show, testing variants
jokes.punchline: She A/B tests which version of telling a child to 'go jump back up your mother' to use as her branded catchphrase, then selects her preferred take with the child's crying as a counterpoint
jokes.explanation: The concept that 'go jump back up your mother' is being professionally workshopped as a branded TV catchphrase — with the child's tears as an intentional production element — is genuinely brilliant. The clinical A/B test framing makes it funnier than if she'd just screamed it. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Sir, this Chiquita banana sticker had been stuck to that ceiling for years. So I finally scraped it off.
jokes.setup: Liz gives Kenneth the day off; he's found at work doing something
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's response to getting a free day is to do 'dream chores' — starting with scraping a banana sticker off a ceiling, which has apparently been bothering only him for years
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Kenneth — his deepest desires are janitorial. The specificity of a Chiquita banana sticker on a ceiling is exactly the kind of detail that makes 30 Rock jokes feel lived-in.

jokes.text: Scrape sticker off ceiling, fix that humming noise only I can hear, organize snack table by food jewishness.
jokes.setup: Liz reads Kenneth's 'dream chores' list aloud
jokes.punchline: 'Organize snack table by food jewishness' — an escalating list where the final item is inexplicable, unverifiable, and yet Kenneth clearly has a confident methodology in mind
jokes.explanation: 'Organize snack table by food jewishness' is the episode's most quotable absurdist joke. It escalates a list of mundane chores to something that raises more questions than it answers — How does Kenneth measure this? On what scale? — while being perfectly specific to his character as a religious Southern man with a complex, unexamined worldview. The ambiguity IS the joke. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Look, if it was my last day on Earth I wouldn't be here, I'd be with Paula, admitting I'm in love with her twin sister.
jokes.setup: Liz is urging Kenneth to do something meaningful with his last day
jokes.punchline: Liz's hypothetical last-day confession reveals a deeply specific and troubling secret love triangle involving a woman named Paula and her twin sister — casually dropped and never elaborated on
jokes.explanation: A beautiful incidental overshare. Liz Lemon is trying to inspire Kenneth and accidentally reveals a complex suppressed secret about her own life. The specificity ('Paula,' 'twin sister') suggests a real situation. Perfectly Liz-coded — she gives away personal trauma while trying to make a completely unrelated point.

jokes.text: Kenneth, we were just out on the Plaza, and four flaming horses rode by. / Reverend Gary says super-gay horses are one of the signs of the apocalypse.
jokes.setup: Liz is trying to convince Kenneth the apocalypse isn't happening
jokes.punchline: Kenneth interprets 'flaming horses' not as horses on fire but as gay horses — which are apparently a specific apocalyptic sign per Reverend Gary's theology
jokes.explanation: Brilliant double meaning — 'flaming' parsed as 'gay' rather than 'on fire.' Kenneth's theology includes 'super-gay horses' as a prophetic sign, which is both a satire of homophobic religious beliefs and completely absurd. 'Super-gay' as a technical theological category is perfect. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: I started a camp for underprivileged kids last summer. We have to drive upstate to see if any of them are still alive.
jokes.setup: Tracy bursts into Liz's office claiming they have a problem
jokes.punchline: The 'problem' is that he started a children's camp and has no idea if the children survived — stated with mild concern rather than alarm
jokes.explanation: 'To see if any of them are still alive' delivered as a practical errand is darkly funny. Tracy's casual indifference to child welfare, framed as a scheduling inconvenience, is peak Tracy Jordan. The use of 'still' implies he knows there's reason for doubt.

jokes.text: Okay, how about this? I'm changing my name. From now on everyone has to address me as 'the gentleman formerly known as rectum.'
jokes.setup: Liz calls the camp a 'Tracy problem' and refuses to engage; Tracy escalates to get her attention
jokes.punchline: Tracy proposes a Prince-style name change to 'the gentleman formerly known as rectum'
jokes.explanation: A Prince reference with Tracy's trademark addition of anatomical vulgarity. 'The gentleman' as a modifier makes 'rectum' funnier — it suggests formal dignity. Very Tracy.

jokes.text: I just got an honorary sheriff's badge, and I'm going to start making real arrests.
jokes.setup: Tracy is escalating threats to get Liz's attention
jokes.punchline: Having an honorary badge and treating it as real law enforcement authority is exactly the kind of Tracy action that would cause genuine chaos
jokes.explanation: Good Tracy escalation joke — his threats are escalating in absurdity and this one implies an entire plotline of mayhem. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: I just realized, I haven't paid taxes in 30 years.
jokes.setup: Tracy continues escalating increasingly alarming self-destructive behavior
jokes.punchline: Tax evasion delivered as a sudden realization rather than a confession — as if this just occurred to him mid-sentence
jokes.explanation: The 'I just realized' framing is what makes this — Tracy isn't announcing it defiantly, he's discovering it in real time. Thirty years suggests this predates any legal income. Good Tracy-specific moment in an escalating list.

jokes.text: You're not doing your job. You're laughing at rectum jokes, you're leaving early. Did we switch brains? Why am I not feeling your boobs? Baah!
jokes.setup: Tracy is accusing Liz of acting out of character
jokes.punchline: Tracy's escalating confusion culminates in him grabbing for Liz's chest to check if he's actually Liz in a Freaky Friday brain swap — complete with sound effect
jokes.explanation: Tracy's Freaky Friday panic is completely in-character and the escalation to physical action (boob check) with a goat sound effect is excellent absurdist physical comedy. The 'Baah!' is a perfect button.

jokes.text: The only show I've ever been on that got a 10.2 was when Mickey Rourke threw me onto the field during the Super Bowl.
jokes.setup: Jack is discussing the show's excellent ratings with Jenna
jokes.punchline: Jenna's only prior 10.2 rating was being physically thrown onto a football field by Mickey Rourke during the Super Bowl — presented as a normal career milestone
jokes.explanation: Jenna's fake celebrity history is a reliable 30 Rock engine, and this is a good specimen. Mickey Rourke throwing her onto a field at the Super Bowl is specific enough to feel like something that might actually appear in a Jenna Maroney Wikipedia entry. The specificity of '10.2' as the exact figure she achieved through assault is wonderful.

jokes.text: B.B. Gun. [as a catchphrase suggestion for Jenna]
jokes.setup: Jack says he had an idea about Jenna's persona
jokes.punchline: d'Fwan interrupts with a completely unexplained 'B.B. Gun' as if it's an obvious answer to an unasked question
jokes.explanation: Absurdist non-sequitur that works because it's so completely unrelated. Two words with no context or follow-up. Low craft but the pure randomness has some charm.

jokes.text: I haven't seen such a unanimously negative response since the Frasier spin-off, hey, Roz.
jokes.setup: Jack is about to deliver bad news about Jenna's focus group results
jokes.punchline: He leads into the bad news by referencing a fake failed Frasier spin-off called 'Hey, Roz' — an NBC meta-joke with perfectly calibrated specificity
jokes.explanation: A sharp meta-NBC joke. 'Hey, Roz' as a fake Frasier spin-off is believable enough as an NBC misfire that it gets a knowing laugh from anyone familiar with the era. The comma placement — announcing the title AFTER the negative comparison — is structurally elegant. Earns 8+ through specificity and meta-comedy craft.

jokes.text: No, Jack. They love to hate me.
jokes.setup: Jack tells Jenna 'they hate you' based on focus testing
jokes.punchline: Jenna reframes complete hatred as a sophisticated audience relationship — 'they love to hate me'
jokes.explanation: A standard celebrity self-delusion joke. It works because of Jenna's delivery and character, but the 'love to hate me' rationalization is a well-worn trope. Functional.

jokes.text: Look, according to Tracy, people are switching minds around here. That's obviously what's happened. So whoever you are, show me Jack's penis.
jokes.setup: Liz finds Jack acting unusually thoughtful
jokes.punchline: Liz decides the only explanation for Jack being emotionally available is a Freaky Friday brain swap — and tests the theory by asking to see Jack's genitalia
jokes.explanation: Liz adopts Tracy's brain-switching theory and escalates it to its logical conclusion — a penis-based identity verification test. The callback to Tracy's earlier panic gives it structure, and Liz's matter-of-fact approach to the request is perfectly in character.

jokes.text: That's for you. [Jack shows something to Liz off-camera, reaction implied]
jokes.setup: Liz asks to see Jack's penis to confirm his identity
jokes.punchline: Jack apparently complies — the audience sees only the timestamp cut, but the 'That's for you' line confirms he showed her something, and her reaction is the joke
jokes.explanation: 'That's for you' combined with the immediate scene cut is a masterclass in comedy economy. The audience fills in the blank. Jack's total willingness to comply — treating the request as entirely reasonable — is the true joke, and the cut prevents any deflation of the moment. Earns 8+ for structure and economy.

jokes.text: Damn, I've got to get more of these. [Liz's reaction after seeing Jack's... something]
jokes.setup: Jack has just shown Liz something in response to the penis request
jokes.punchline: Liz's reaction ('I've got to get more of these') is ambiguous — it could refer to the penis, or Jack may have shown her something completely different (like a card or badge). The ambiguity is the joke.
jokes.explanation: The misdirection works either way — whether Jack showed his penis (making Liz's enthusiastic response funny) or something mundane (undercutting the whole setup). The ambiguity is intentional and gives the audience room to choose their preferred interpretation.

jokes.text: After 6 years, I've cheered up Miss Lemon. That was on your list?
jokes.setup: Jack notes with satisfaction that Liz is in a good mood
jokes.punchline: The revelation that 'cheer up Liz Lemon' was an actual item on Jack's to-do list — implying it was a years-long project requiring dedicated effort
jokes.explanation: Nicely self-aware about the Jack/Liz relationship dynamic over six seasons. Jack's pride at finally checking off 'cheer up Lemon' after six years of effort is both funny and, in a 30 Rock way, touching.

jokes.text: Well, enjoy it while you can, because tomorrow, you're going to women's hell. Uh, also, FYI, women's hell is the same as aroused dog heaven.
jokes.setup: Liz says she's in a good place; Kenneth responds about the afterlife
jokes.punchline: 'Women's hell is the same as aroused dog heaven' — Kenneth's theology includes a specific and disturbing overlap between the worst place for women and the best place for male dogs, delivered as an FYI
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a legitimate 30 Rock all-timer. The joke operates on multiple levels: (1) the horrifying implication of what 'women's hell' would contain for dogs, (2) Kenneth's casual delivery of this theological insight as an afterthought ('also, FYI'), (3) it's uniquely Kenneth — only he would have mapped out the cosmological Venn diagram of hell and dog heaven. Highly original, perfectly structured, and deeply character-specific. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor — arguably better. Earns its 8+.

jokes.text: Have you ever been in love? / Only while playing tennis. / I'm kidding. I've never played tennis.
jokes.setup: Jack asks Kenneth if he's ever been in love
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's cryptic tennis-love connection is immediately undermined by the revelation that he's never played tennis — so the romantic metaphor has no referent
jokes.explanation: A beautiful three-beat joke. Beat 1: intriguing answer. Beat 2: 'I'm kidding' — sets up an explanation. Beat 3: 'I've never played tennis' — the 'joke' is that there is no joke, just a confession that the previous statement was meaningless. Kenneth's life is more poignant for the absence of both love AND tennis. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: Well, does falling off a bridge in a horse cart count? [when asked if Kenneth has ever been in an airplane]
jokes.setup: Jack asks if Kenneth has ever been in an airplane
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's frame of reference for 'flying' is so pre-modern that he conflates airplane travel with horse-cart bridge accidents
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Kenneth — he's from a place and time where horse carts and bridges are relevant personal history. The joke also implies a traumatic story he's treating as completely routine. Good character-specific absurdism.

jokes.text: Sir, I've never even seen the ocean. / Never? Kenneth, that's insane.
jokes.setup: Jack asks Kenneth if he's ever seen a beach sunrise
jokes.punchline: Kenneth has never seen the ocean at all — delivered with complete serenity, prompting genuine shock from Jack
jokes.explanation: The emotional core of the Kenneth plotline, but it functions as comedy through the juxtaposition of Kenneth's contentment and Jack's horror. Jack calling it 'insane' while himself being a plutocrat who tortures reality show children is a nice irony.

jokes.text: You know what? I have seen the ocean on a can of tuna. Newsflash, Kenneth! Everybody get down!
jokes.setup: Jack is having an epiphany about Kenneth never having seen the ocean
jokes.punchline: Jack's grandiose speech is suddenly interrupted by him apparently diving/rolling dramatically — for reasons the transcript implies but doesn't explain
jokes.explanation: 'I have seen the ocean on a can of tuna' is a lovely incidental image — Jack Donaghy's point of oceanic reference is a canned fish label. The 'Everybody get down!' seems to transition into the revelation that Lutz was pretending to be a monster, gaining rewatch value in context.

jokes.text: Aah! Redire ad abyssum! Princeps tenebrarum! Ow! It's me, Lutz.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is convinced the apocalypse is happening; something scary appears
jokes.punchline: The 'beast of the apocalypse' is revealed to be Lutz, who was apparently pretending to be a demon using Latin phrases — then breaking character with 'Ow! It's me, Lutz'
jokes.explanation: The Latin exorcism phrases followed by the completely deflating 'Ow! It's me, Lutz' is a good structure. Lutz breaking the bit because of physical pain is perfectly in character for the show's least competent schemer.

jokes.text: Tracy, how do nice people dress? / Socks on their hands, no belt, roller skates.
jokes.setup: Jenna asks Tracy what nice people dress like, seeking advice on softening her TV persona.
jokes.punchline: Tracy's authoritative answer — socks on their hands, no belt, roller skates — describes not a nice person but a chaotic hobo clown.
jokes.explanation: Tracy's image of 'nice' people is a specific and surprising absurdity — the 'no belt' detail between the bizarre hand-socks and roller skates is what makes it funny. Each item in the list is a deliberate misfire. Tracy is giving sincere advice based on his genuinely alien understanding of social norms.

jokes.text: Breathtaking. You're the wind beneath my wings. [Jenna, now being 'nice' to kids]
jokes.setup: Jenna is attempting to be 'nice' to child contestants after Jack's directive.
jokes.punchline: Her version of 'nice' is stilted, robotic, and deeply insincere — 'breathtaking, you're the wind beneath my wings' sounds like she's reading from a compliment template.
jokes.explanation: The cringe comedy of watching Jenna try to be nice — deploying the most generic, clichéd compliments with zero authentic warmth — is effective. 'You're the wind beneath my wings' to a random child is perfectly hollow.

jokes.text: Because I will not go back to putting hair extensions on dogs.
jokes.setup: d'Fwan is warning Jack not to mess with the reality show format
jokes.punchline: His previous career (or threat of career regression) involved putting hair extensions on dogs — presumably as some kind of pet styling business
jokes.explanation: A very specific professional history that implies a whole world of dog hair extension salons that d'Fwan is desperate not to return to. The specificity (hair extensions, not grooming — not even wigs, but extensions) is what makes it funny.

jokes.text: Next week Jay-Z was going to do a duet with one of the spinning chairs from the Voice, and the chair just pulled out.
jokes.setup: Jack is explaining how high-stakes the show's problems have become
jokes.punchline: A spinning chair from The Voice was booked as a celebrity duet partner for Jay-Z and has backed out — treating an inanimate piece of furniture as a sentient talent with agency
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a highlight of 30 Rock's absurdist meta-television comedy. The premise elevates The Voice's spinning chairs from a gimmick to a celebrity in their own right, capable of scheduling conflicts and professional commitments. 'The chair just pulled out' is delivered with complete seriousness. The joke works on multiple levels: reality TV satire, celebrity culture satire, and pure surrealism. Highly quotable. Earns 8+ with ease.

jokes.text: Did you see what happened here? We turned an argument into an opportunity to become better friends.
jokes.setup: Jenna and Jack have just argued about the show
jokes.punchline: Jenna reframes their conflict as a heartwarming friendship moment — clearly modeling the behavior she's supposed to perform on the children's show
jokes.explanation: The joke here is Jenna involuntarily slipping into the nice-Jenna mode she'd been discussing, then presenting it as a genuine insight. Functional but not exceptional.

jokes.text: You're at work before Miss Lemon? Now, that's a sign of the apocalypse.
jokes.setup: Tracy arrives at work before Liz, which apparently never happens.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth, who has been watching for apocalyptic signs all day, finds one in the mundane workplace observation that Tracy beat Liz to the office.
jokes.explanation: A nice callback that connects the A-plot (Liz's weird behavior) to the C-plot (Kenneth's apocalypse) with an economical line. Kenneth's genuine conviction makes it land. Good structural integration.

jokes.text: Jack explains to Liddy that Variety called the show 'Boffo' and 'they don't throw that word around lightly' — treating a trade publication review as an infant's required reading
jokes.setup: Jack is having a formal meeting with his infant daughter to explain the realities of show business
jokes.punchline: Jack cites Variety's 'Boffo' review as if it's evidence a baby would weigh in her moral calculus
jokes.explanation: The premise of Jack treating Liddy as a business partner he must brief on ratings is the engine of this scene. Citing Variety specifically — and noting the magazine's judicious use of 'boffo' — is peak Jack Donaghy character comedy.

jokes.text: And if you think I'm going to turn my back on a 10.2/4.2 in the demo just because I feel bad... just because those kids had the same scared look on their faces that you had when that dog got too close to your stroller.
jokes.setup: Jack is arguing to Liddy that business comes before feelings
jokes.punchline: He makes the comparison between terrified TV children and his daughter's dog-stroller fear — and the comparison breaks him
jokes.explanation: The moment Jack's argument collapses is both funny and genuinely moving. The comedy comes from his attempt to dehumanize the situation running directly into his own humanity — triggered by the specific memory of Liddy's scared face near a dog. The precision of 'too close to your stroller' is the detail that makes it.

jokes.text: What are you doing, Liddy? Are you touching my hand because you're a baby and you're developing your fine motor skills? Or are you trying to tell me something?
jokes.setup: Jack has been having a full boardroom-style meeting with his infant daughter about the ethics of the children's show
jokes.punchline: Jack sincerely asks his infant if she's communicating a moral message or just doing baby stuff — treating infant motor development as a plausible alternative explanation
jokes.explanation: The entire Liddy meeting scene is a sustained joke, but this moment is the best beat within it — Jack giving the baby the benefit of the doubt that she might just be developing motor skills rather than delivering wisdom. His scientific alternative hypothesis makes the mysticism funnier.

jokes.text: Mommy. / Did you say 'money'? / Mommy. / Yes, money. Are you telling me that money's more important than doing what's right? That I should keep on doing the show? / I want mommy. / I want money too!
jokes.setup: Jack has asked Liddy a moral question about the show; the baby says her first word
jokes.punchline: Jack mishears 'Mommy' as 'money' three times and builds an entire moral framework around the infant's advice to 'keep doing the show for money' — all while the baby is just asking for her mother
jokes.explanation: A perfectly escalating joke that's also a sharp character piece. Jack's selective hearing (mommy → money) is plausible for a man whose internal monologue is entirely financial. The escalation — one mishearing, then a second confirmation, then 'I want money too!' as a bonding moment with his baby — is beautifully structured. Earns 8+ through character integration and escalation.

jokes.text: Hey, think how disappointed I am. I mean, I'm the one who had to nude-baptize all those teens.
jokes.setup: Someone expresses disappointment that the show is being cancelled
jokes.punchline: 'I'm the one who had to nude-baptize all those teens' — a completely unexplained, deeply alarming statement about what this person has been doing in service of the show
jokes.explanation: The comedy is entirely in the unexplained specificity — 'nude-baptize' is alarming enough, but 'all those teens' implies scale. The speaker presents this as a legitimate hardship that earns them extra sympathy, without any awareness that this is not a normal thing. Dark and quotable.

jokes.text: Make fun of the super-handsome guy who believed too much.
jokes.setup: Kenneth tells Jack to go ahead and make fun of him for believing the world was ending.
jokes.punchline: His self-description as 'the super-handsome guy who believed too much' is the joke — Kenneth's total lack of self-awareness about his appearance, combined with framing religious credulity as a form of excess love.
jokes.explanation: 'Super-handsome' as Kenneth's self-assessment is a running joke in the show — his obliviousness to how he actually looks. 'Believed too much' as his one flaw is both pathetic and oddly noble. Good economy and strong character integration.

jokes.text: You three are in a time-out. Everybody in the van!
jokes.setup: Liz has caught Frank, Toofer, and Lutz tormenting Kenneth with fake apocalypse theatrics
jokes.punchline: Liz punishes grown men by putting them in a 'time-out' and herding them into a van like children
jokes.explanation: Liz's maternal management of the writers' room is a reliable joke engine, and 'Everybody in the van' as a punishment for adult men is a good image. Functional character comedy.

jokes.text: You three are in a time-out. Everybody in the van!
jokes.setup: Frank, Toofer, and Lutz have been revealed as the ones who faked the apocalyptic signs to prank Kenneth.
jokes.punchline: Kenneth's punishment — a 'time-out' and mandatory van confinement — treats grown adults like misbehaving children, delivered with complete authority.
jokes.explanation: Kenneth's parental authority over the writers is a recurring dynamic. 'Everybody in the van!' as punishment is both absurd (what is the van?) and delivered with total conviction. Works as a character beat.

jokes.text: Liz Lemon is a crack whore. / Probably not, but continue.
jokes.setup: Tracy has been investigating Liz's strange behavior and returns with his conclusion
jokes.punchline: Jenna's 'Probably not, but continue' — she doesn't dismiss it outright, allowing for a small probability of crack-whoredom
jokes.explanation: 'Probably not, but continue' is a perfectly Jenna line — she's just open-minded enough about Liz's crack-whoredom to not fully rule it out. The construction ('probably not' rather than 'definitely not') is everything. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: She went down to Penn Station. And not the fun stationery store up on the Upper East Side. The skeezy one with trains.
jokes.setup: Tracy is recounting his surveillance of Liz at Penn Station
jokes.punchline: Tracy clarifies that Penn Station is 'the skeezy one with trains,' as opposed to the 'fun stationery store' he apparently prefers — revealing his total unfamiliarity with how New York infrastructure works
jokes.explanation: A spectacular Tracy Jordan joke. The premise that Tracy navigates New York partly by misidentifying train stations as stationery stores is both deeply absurd and somehow internally consistent with his worldview. 'The skeezy one with trains' as a descriptor for a major transit hub is perfect. Earns 8+ through originality and character integration.

jokes.text: Are you sure it was Liz Lemon and not present day Sally Field?
jokes.setup: Tracy reports that Liz was at Penn Station in suspicious circumstances
jokes.punchline: Jenna suggests that a woman looking rough enough to be mistaken for a crack whore could just as easily be 'present day Sally Field' — a specific, mean celebrity comparison
jokes.explanation: 'Present day Sally Field' is the key modifier — it acknowledges Sally Field's enduring fame while gently suggesting her appearance is now in the Penn Station crack-whore zone. The specificity makes it funnier than a generic 'old lady' comparison.

jokes.text: She's been acting all weird. All relaxed and not angry. Well, it has been two days, and she hasn't once stormed in here carping about how all the destructive hurricanes get female names.
jokes.setup: Tracy and Jenna note Liz has been acting strangely since Kwanzaa
jokes.punchline: Liz's 'weird' behavior = relaxed and not angry; her baseline includes frequent rants about hurricane naming conventions being sexist
jokes.explanation: The hurricane-naming feminist complaint as a specific Liz Lemon recurring grievance is very character-specific. It's the kind of detail that makes Liz feel like a real person with consistent (if absurd) political hobby-horses.

jokes.text: Oh, Tracy, this is dexoprex. My mother takes it for joint pain. Her wrist was starting to bother her from slapping busboys.
jokes.setup: Tracy found mysterious pills in Liz's trash and assumed they were cocaine
jokes.punchline: The pills are joint pain medication — belonging to Jenna's mother, whose wrist pain stems from habitual busboy-slapping
jokes.explanation: A beautiful three-layer joke: (1) the drug reveal is mundane, (2) it belongs to Jenna's mother, (3) the wrist injury came from busboy-slapping. The specificity of 'busboys' (not waiters, not random people — busboys specifically) implies an ongoing pattern of class-based violence that Jenna relates completely without shame. Excellent.

jokes.text: So it's not the Bandito Blanco? A name for cocaine I just made up?
jokes.setup: Jenna explains the pills aren't drugs
jokes.punchline: Tracy clarifies that 'Bandito Blanco' is a cocaine name he invented on the spot — suggesting he was also conducting a drug-naming exercise simultaneously
jokes.explanation: Tracy's clarification that this is a brand-new cocaine name he coined in real time is vintage Tracy — he's simultaneously conducting the investigation AND inventing drug terminology. 'A name for cocaine I just made up' as an explanatory parenthetical is perfectly economical.

jokes.text: The Manhattan center for penis enlargement? I know because my friend goes there. His name is Tracy.
jokes.setup: Jenna asks Tracy what building is next to Penn Station
jokes.punchline: Tracy guesses 'the Manhattan center for penis enlargement' and then immediately outs himself as a client, then tries to cover with 'His name is Tracy' — as if that's a different Tracy
jokes.explanation: Three-beat joke with an excellent final beat: Tracy guesses a fake clinic, immediately reveals personal familiarity, then offers the flimsiest possible cover story. 'His name is Tracy' as a deflection while everyone knows it's him is perfectly structured self-incrimination.

jokes.text: Ladies and gentlemen, please welcome the WNBA's most popular dance team, 'the Timeless Torches.'
jokes.setup: The mystery of Liz's secret hobby is finally revealed
jokes.punchline: Liz has been secretly dancing with 'the Timeless Torches' — the WNBA's most popular dance team, whose name implies they are for older women
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the episode's mystery. 'The Timeless Torches' as a name for a dance troupe of older women is perfectly calibrated — 'timeless' is a euphemism for 'old,' and 'torches' has a slightly desperate, still-burning quality. And it IS the WNBA's 'most popular' team, a low bar that adds to the sadness/joy of the reveal.

jokes.text: Oh, God! So much grapevining!
jokes.setup: Tracy and Jenna watch Liz perform with the dance troupe
jokes.punchline: Jenna's horrified reaction to the dancing is that there's 'so much grapevining' — the grapevine being an extremely basic and uncool dance move
jokes.explanation: Jenna's specific horror at the grapevine move — a staple of low-intensity group aerobics — is a great detail. It's the perfect dance for this group and the perfect reason for Jenna's theatrical disgust. 'So much' implies the quantity is the real problem.

jokes.text: It's so beautiful. A mermaid! / Dude, those are diapers.
jokes.setup: Kenneth is moved to tears watching Liz dance with the Timeless Torches
jokes.punchline: Kenneth sees a mermaid; Tracy corrects that he's looking at diapers (presumably adult protective garments worn by some dancers)
jokes.explanation: A sublime exchange. Kenneth's wonder at the beauty of the performance; Tracy's flat correction that what looks like a mermaid tail is actually adult diapers. The contrast between Kenneth's romanticism and Tracy's blunt realism is perfectly timed, and 'dude' as an opener makes Tracy sound almost gentle. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: The joy of movement, exercise, 10% off arena snacks with your torch card.
jokes.setup: Jack lists the reasons Liz has been happy and distracted
jokes.punchline: Liz confirms them all including '10% off arena snacks with your torch card' — revealing that a minor concession discount was a meaningful factor in her joy
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'joy of movement' and 'exercise' (meaningful things) to '10% off arena snacks' (extremely specific minor perk) as equally weighted sources of happiness is perfectly Liz Lemon. The torch card as a membership benefit that brings her genuine joy is deeply character-specific.

jokes.text: You're going alone, to the 9:10 showing of Garry Marshall's New Year's Eve. You've waited five weeks to see it, to make sure that you wouldn't contribute to it being the number one movie in America. You'll say you're seeing it ironically, and yet you'll tear up when Ashton Kutcher kisses Lea Michele. / You know me. / I love it when the swarthy girl gets the guy.
jokes.setup: Jack predicts exactly what Liz is about to do on her evening out
jokes.punchline: Liz confirms everything, and her defense of the movie is that she loves 'when the swarthy girl gets the guy' — describing Lea Michele with 'swarthy' as a compliment
jokes.explanation: The callback to Jack predicting Liz's holiday makes this land even harder — he's done it again with her movie plans. Each detail escalates the joke: waiting five weeks to avoid contributing to box office numbers is neurotic in a very Liz way; 'you'll say you're seeing it ironically, and yet you'll tear up' is devastating. 'Swarthy girl' as Liz's affectionate identification with Lea Michele is a beautiful final beat. Earns 8+.

jokes.text: You'll say you're seeing it ironically, and yet you'll tear up when Ashton Kutcher kisses Lea Michele.
jokes.setup: Jack continues predicting Liz's movie experience.
jokes.punchline: Liz's ironic cover story will collapse into genuine emotion at the rom-com payoff — specifically Ashton Kutcher kissing Lea Michele.
jokes.explanation: The 'seeing it ironically' is a perfect Liz Lemon self-defense mechanism, and the tears betraying genuine investment is a running theme of her character (she loves schmaltz). The specific casting choice of Ashton Kutcher and Lea Michele for the emotional moment adds topical absurdism.

jokes.text: My name is Bob. I'm 61 years old. My favorite move is the shoulder shake. / My name is Joyce. I'm 63 years young. My favorite move is the Dougie. / I'm Liz. I'm 39, for the third time, and my favorite move is sunset arms.
jokes.setup: Timeless Torches members introduce themselves in a talking-head style segment
jokes.punchline: '39, for the third time' — Liz's running lie about her age, and 'sunset arms' as an official dance move name that evokes elderly melancholy
jokes.explanation: '39, for the third time' is a great Liz Lemon detail — she's 39 and has been 39 multiple times. 'Sunset arms' as her signature move implies something vaguely autumnal and fading. Joyce being '63 years young' and doing the Dougie is a good running-gag escalator.

jokes.text: Hi, I'm Lewis. I'm a grandfather from the Dominican Republic, and my favorite move is the lift. / Sorry, Lewis.
jokes.setup: Timeless Torches members are naming their favorite moves
jokes.punchline: Lewis's move is 'the lift' — and Liz's immediate apologetic response suggests the lift has gone badly and Lewis is perhaps on the floor
jokes.explanation: Two words ('Sorry, Lewis') are the entire joke, and the audience fills in the physical comedy. An elderly man attempting a Dirty Dancing lift with Liz Lemon ending in collapse is implied entirely by her apology. Perfect economy for a visual gag.

jokes.text: Nice try, Liz. Dance like nobody's watchin'!
jokes.setup: Liz attempts the lift with Lewis and it goes wrong
jokes.punchline: Someone calls out the episode's titular quote as encouragement, completing the thematic frame
jokes.explanation: A satisfying thematic button. The episode's title pays off here as genuine encouragement rather than corporate inspiration, giving the absurdist tampon quote a warm landing. Not exceptional craft but effective closure.

tmdb_overview: Tracy becomes frustrated in his attempts to anger Liz. Jack questions the family value of the network's new talent competition and Kenneth awaits the Rapture.
insight: Season 6 opener lands 87.2 with absurdist density—51 jokes in 23 minutes sustains peak-era chaos.
